hops.afterHeading: The fibre that prefers a caress
hops.title: Fifty years from a cat's leg to a human forehead
hops.text: In 1939, the Swedish physiologist Yngve Zotterman recorded from a nerve serving the hairy skin of a cat's leg and caught slow, unmyelinated C fibres firing to gentle stroking. Similar fibres turned up in nonhuman primates, yet in 1990 Magnus Nordin could still write that they had not been proven to exist in people. In that paper he described sliding a tungsten electrode into a forehead nerve in human volunteers. Eight slow C fibres answered touches lighter than a quarter of a gram. A slow sweep of cotton wool drove them briskly, and rapid strokes made them fire less. The cat's gentle-touch fibres had been in human skin all along.

sources.citation: Moore et al., Journal of Physiology (2025), 603(16):4593-4608 (citing Zotterman, 1939, and Nordin, 1990).

image.caption: Slow touch fibres recorded in a cat in 1939 were described in detail in human skin in 1990.

hops.afterHeading: Take the input away: what people show
hops.title: Your own stroke versus a friend's
hops.text: Close your eyes and slowly stroke the hairy back of your left forearm with your right hand, taking about three seconds to cross ten centimetres. Then, eyes still closed, have a friend copy the stroke and notice how the two feel. In 2019, Rebecca Boehme and colleagues compared self-stroking with strokes from an experimenter who mimicked each volunteer's motion. Another person's touch activated the insula and somatosensory cortex; self-touch deactivated the insula. On average, feeling a light filament press took nearly three times the force during self-stroking as during the experimenter's strokes, and over a hundred times the force with no stroking. Whose hand made the stroke mattered.

sources.citation: Boehme, Hauser, Gerling, Heilig & Olausson, PNAS (2019), 116(6):2290-2299.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two students at a wooden table, one gently stroking the back of the other's forearm while the recipient keeps their eyes closed.
image.caption: Self-stroking quieted the insula and made a light press harder to feel than another person's stroke did.

hops.afterHeading: From skin to reward-like outcomes in mice
hops.title: Dairy cows pushing a weighted gate to reach a brush
hops.text: A cow cannot fill in a pleasantness scale, so Emilie McConnachie and colleagues in British Columbia analyzed ten Holsteins trained to push a weighted gate. From seven kilograms, they added weight until no cow pushed through, though the final brush round ended early. Behind the gate was a mechanical brush that rotated on contact, fresh feed, or an empty space. The cows pushed similar weights for the brush and fresh feed, though under different test setups, and significantly less for the empty space. The gate records the heaviest load a cow opens; a mouse's place preference tracks change in time spent in a chamber. Neither shows how a touch feels.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A black-and-white dairy cow leaning contentedly against a large yellow rotating barn brush behind a weighted wooden gate.
image.caption: Holstein cows pushed similar gate weights to reach a brush as to reach fresh feed.

audio.title: Warm strokes, a cat's leg, and a weighted barn gate
audio.transcript:
Nobody checks a stopwatch before stroking a baby's arm, yet people seem to land on speeds that activate C-tactile fibres. In two thousand sixteen, Ilona Croy and colleagues tracked stroking speeds in three groups of volunteers: forty-five people stroking an artificial arm, thirty-two stroking a partner, and eleven parents stroking their babies. People moved noticeably faster across the fake arm, whereas everyone stroking a partner or a baby used speeds that can activate C-tactile fibres. Speed is only half the recipe, though. Two years earlier, Rochelle Ackerley and colleagues recorded single C-tactile axons in human forearms while a computer-controlled probe stroked at eighteen, thirty-two, and forty-two degrees Celsius. In the fast, myelinated hair fibres they tested, firing simply rose with speed, and the study found no clear temperature effect. The slow C-tactile fibres were pickier. Their average firing peaked at three centimetres per second with the probe at thirty-two degrees Celsius, close to typical arm skin temperature. At most of the slower speeds, thirty-two degrees drove higher firing than the cooler or warmer settings, though at the three-centimetre peak the edge over the warm probe was not statistically significant. And only at thirty-two degrees did their average firing show a statistically significant correlation with how pleasant separate volunteers rated the same strokes.

Strangely, physiologists went half a century before these fibres were characterized in detail in human skin. Back in nineteen thirty-nine, the Swedish researcher Yngve Zotterman recorded from a nerve serving a cat's hairy leg and caught slow, unmyelinated C fibres firing to gentle stroking. Similar fibres turned up in nonhuman primates, yet in nineteen ninety Magnus Nordin in Uppsala could still write that they had not been proven to exist in people. In that paper, he reported recordings made by slipping a fine tungsten electrode into a forehead nerve in human volunteers. Of eleven C fibres he recorded, eight were gentle-touch units, answering touches lighter than a quarter of a gram; the other three were pain fibres. A slow sweep with a wisp of cotton wool drove the touch units briskly, while rapid strokes cut their firing back. Those slow gentle-touch fibres had been sitting in our foreheads all along.

Of course, you can ask a volunteer in Uppsala how a stroke feels. You cannot hand a rating scale to a mouse, or to a dairy cow. Indoor dairy cows often have nothing good to scratch against, and some farms install mechanical brushes that start rotating on contact. In two thousand sixteen, Emilie McConnachie and colleagues in British Columbia measured how much Holstein cows actually wanted one, analyzing ten cows that had learned to shove open a weighted push-gate. Testing began with seven kilograms on the pulley, and the researchers added weight until no cow pushed it open, except that the final brush round ended three days early as the cows approached calving. The cows worked for three options: the mechanical brush, fresh feed, or an empty space. They pushed significantly less weight for the empty space and similar weights for the brush and fresh feed, even though they had days to try the gate for the brush and only fifteen minutes per session to open it for thirty seconds of feed. Just like the mouse studies in this lesson, a heavy gate cannot tell us what a cow feels inside. But it gives science a clean, measurable price tag for a good scratch.
